note: Use of English round 2: 2 comprehension passages, 2 cloze passages (10 gaps each), sentence interpretation, synonyms/antonyms in context, basic grammar, word stress, rhymes, sounds, emphatic stress. Retires bare-word synonym/antonym items and one-line recall.

passages.title: Okada ban in the city
passages.text: When the state government banned commercial motorcycles from the city centre, the reaction was immediate and divided. Office workers who had relied on the machines to weave through traffic suddenly found themselves spending two hours on journeys that used to take twenty minutes. Riders, most of them young men who had borrowed money to buy their motorcycles, gathered outside the secretariat in protest. Yet hospital records told a different story. Within a month, the number of accident victims arriving at the emergency unit of the teaching hospital had fallen by almost half, and the orthopaedic ward, once nicknamed 'the okada ward', had empty beds for the first time in years. The commissioner for transport insisted that the policy was never about punishing anyone. 'We are asking a simple question,' she said. 'How many broken legs is a fast journey worth?' Critics reply that the question is unfair: the government banned the motorcycles without first providing the buses it had promised. Both sides, it seems, agree on one thing – that the city cannot go on as it was.

passages.title: The old librarian
passages.text: Mr Adekunle had run the town library for thirty-one years, and in all that time he had never once raised his voice. He did not need to. A single glance over the rim of his spectacles was enough to silence the rowdiest schoolboy. The children called him 'Baba Book' behind his back, and, although he pretended not to know, the name pleased him more than the certificate of merit the local government had given him. When the new digital library opened across the road, with its air-conditioning and its rows of glowing screens, everybody expected the old building to close. Instead, something curious happened. The teenagers went to the new place for their assignments and came back to the old one to read. 'Over there you find information,' one girl explained. 'Here you find Baba Book.' Mr Adekunle, who was listening from behind the shelves, took off his spectacles and cleaned them for a very long time.

The principal, a tall woman with a voice that needed no microphone, reminded them that success in the coming examinations would [3] on steady work rather than last-minute [4]. She then introduced three new teachers, one of [5] had come all the way from Sokoto. After the assembly, the students [6] to their classrooms, where timetables were [7] and textbooks shared out. By noon the rain had stopped, and the compound rang with the [8] of voices as friends who had not seen one another for two months exchanged holiday stories. It was, everyone agreed, a promising [9] to the term, even if the [10] of homework that evening came as an unwelcome reminder that the holidays were truly over.

passages.title: Cloze passage: Saving for the future
passages.text: Many young Nigerians find it difficult to save money, not because they earn too little but because they have never [1] the habit. Financial experts advise that the moment a salary is paid, a fixed [2] – say ten per cent – should be moved into a separate account before any bill is [3]. This method, often called 'paying yourself first', works because it removes the [4] to spend. Over time the small amounts [5] into a sum large enough to meet an emergency or to [6] a business. Experts also warn against borrowing to buy things that lose value, such as phones and clothes, since the [7] on such loans can swallow a third of one's income. [8], they recommend keeping a simple record of daily expenses; people are usually [9] to discover how much they spend on snacks and airtime. Saving, in the end, is less about mathematics than about [10].

questions.C: were written by a different person

questions.subject: Use of English

questions.A: request accurate accident statistics from hospitals
questions.B: admit that the government's ban has failed
questions.C: mock the riders for their reckless driving
questions.D: suggest that speed should not be bought with injuries

questions.A: waited far too long before banning motorcycles
questions.B: refused to publish the hospital records
questions.C: punished office workers instead of riders
questions.D: did not provide alternative transport before the ban

questions.subject: Use of English

questions.explanation: 'A single glance over the rim of his spectacles was enough to silence the rowdiest schoolboy.'

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The nickname 'Baba Book'
questions.D: was given by the local government
questions.explanation: He 'pretended not to know', but the name 'pleased him more than the certificate of merit'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'curious', as used in the passage, means
questions.explanation: Here 'curious' describes the surprising turn of events, not a person's desire to know.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The girl's remark 'Here you find Baba Book' implies that
questions.A: the human warmth of the librarian matters as much as information
questions.B: the new digital library has no trained staff
questions.C: the old library has far more books than the new one
questions.D: the teenagers are uncomfortable with computers
questions.explanation: She contrasts 'information' (available across the road) with the person — what draws them back is Mr Adekunle himself.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Mr Adekunle cleaned his spectacles 'for a very long time' because he
questions.A: could no longer see well without them
questions.B: was looking for an excuse to leave the room
questions.C: was too annoyed with the girl to reply
questions.D: was deeply moved and hiding his emotion
questions.explanation: Cleaning his glasses at length is a way of concealing tears or emotion after hearing the compliment.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Bola would have won the election but for the last-minute defection of her supporters.
questions.A: Bola lost because her supporters left her at the last minute
questions.B: Bola won the election in spite of the defection
questions.C: Bola's supporters helped her win at the last minute
questions.D: Bola did not contest the election
questions.explanation: 'Would have won ... but for X' means she did NOT win, and X was the reason.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Not even the principal could persuade Tunde to apologise.
questions.A: The principal did not make any attempt to persuade Tunde to apologise
questions.B: Tunde eventually apologised, but only to the principal himself
questions.C: Tunde succeeded in persuading the principal to apologise instead
questions.D: Tunde refused to apologise despite pressure from everyone, including the principal
questions.explanation: 'Not even X could' stresses that X, the most likely to succeed, also failed — Tunde stayed stubborn.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The manager's remarks were as unnecessary as they were unkind.
questions.A: The remarks were both unnecessary and unkind
questions.B: The remarks were kind but unnecessary
questions.C: The remarks were necessary but unkind
questions.D: The manager did not make any remarks
questions.explanation: 'As X as Y' states that both qualities apply equally.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Much as I admire Chinedu, I cannot support his decision.
questions.A: I admire Chinedu, so I support his decision
questions.B: I support Chinedu because I admire him
questions.C: I neither admire Chinedu nor support him
questions.D: Although I admire Chinedu, I do not support his decision
questions.explanation: 'Much as' means 'although' — a concession followed by a contrast.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The new road is anything but smooth.
questions.A: The road is not smooth at all
questions.D: The road has not been built
questions.explanation: 'Anything but X' means definitely not X.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Ngozi is too proud to ask for help.
questions.A: Ngozi is proud of asking for help
questions.C: Ngozi's pride prevents her from asking for help
questions.D: Ngozi is proud because she was helped
questions.explanation: 'Too X to Y' means so X that Y does not happen.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Had the goalkeeper not slipped, the match would have ended in a draw.
questions.A: The match ended in a draw
questions.D: The goalkeeper slipped and his team lost
questions.explanation: An unreal past condition: the slip happened, and because of it the match did not end in a draw — the goalkeeper's side conceded and lost.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: It was with a heavy heart that the chief announced the cancellation of the festival.
questions.A: The chief was unhappy to cancel the festival
questions.C: The chief was happy to cancel the festival
questions.explanation: 'With a heavy heart' means sadly or reluctantly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Emeka's business is barely keeping its head above water.
questions.A: The business is doing very well
questions.C: The business is located near water
questions.D: The business is only just surviving
questions.explanation: 'Keep one's head above water' means to survive with difficulty, usually financially.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: No sooner had the teacher left than the class erupted in noise.
questions.A: The class became noisy immediately after the teacher left
questions.B: The class was noisy before the teacher left
questions.C: The teacher left because the class was noisy
questions.D: The class remained quiet after the teacher left
questions.explanation: 'No sooner ... than' means as soon as / immediately after.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The governor's speech was full of PLATITUDES about unity and progress.
questions.explanation: A platitude is a remark that has been used so often it has become meaningless.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The committee's findings CORROBORATED the witness's account.
questions.explanation: To corroborate is to support with additional evidence — to confirm.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The old bridge is in a PRECARIOUS condition.
questions.explanation: Precarious means dangerously insecure or unstable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: He made a FUTILE attempt to stop the fire with a bucket of water.
questions.explanation: Futile means producing no result — pointless.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The two countries have a CORDIAL relationship.
questions.explanation: Cordial means warm and friendly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The lecturer gave a SUCCINCT summary of the chapter.
questions.explanation: Succinct means expressed briefly and clearly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The chairman's decision was final and IRREVOCABLE.
questions.explanation: Irrevocable means impossible to reverse or cancel.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: She was RETICENT about her plans for the future.
questions.explanation: A reticent person does not reveal thoughts or feelings readily.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The soldiers showed remarkable FORTITUDE during the siege.
questions.explanation: Fortitude is courage and strength in the face of pain or difficulty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The auditor found several DISCREPANCIES in the accounts.
questions.explanation: A discrepancy is a difference between things that should agree.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The witness gave a CANDID account of what happened.
questions.explanation: Candid means frank and honest; the opposite is evasive.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The rebels were finally SUBDUED by the army.
questions.explanation: Subdued means brought under control or quietened; the opposite is roused (stirred up).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The new policy has been widely CONDEMNED.
questions.explanation: To condemn is to express strong disapproval; the opposite is to praise.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The soil in this region is remarkably FERTILE.
questions.explanation: Fertile land produces abundant crops; barren land produces little or nothing.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The patient's condition is now STABLE.
questions.explanation: Stable means not likely to change or get worse; critical means dangerously unstable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The minister's answer was DELIBERATELY vague.
questions.explanation: Deliberately (on purpose) is the opposite of accidentally.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: He is known for his LAVISH spending on parties.
questions.explanation: Lavish means extravagant; frugal means sparing and economical.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Her handwriting is LEGIBLE.
questions.explanation: Legible means clear enough to read; the opposite is illegible.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The judge was praised for his LENIENT sentence.
questions.explanation: Lenient means merciful or mild; the opposite is harsh.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The organisation operates in a TRANSPARENT manner.
questions.explanation: Transparent here means open and honest; the opposite is secretive.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The news ____ so shocking that nobody spoke for a minute.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Each of the candidates ____ given a form to fill.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular: each ... was.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: This is the woman ____ son won the scholarship.
questions.explanation: Possession ('her son') requires 'whose'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Between you and ____, the principal is not happy with the result.
questions.explanation: After a preposition ('between') the object form 'me' is required.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She has been working here ____ 2019.
questions.explanation: 'Since' + a point in time; 'for' + a length of time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The children enjoyed ____ at the beach.
questions.explanation: The reflexive plural is 'themselves'; 'theirselves' and 'themself' are not standard.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Neither of the two answers ____ correct.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' (of two) takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The teacher, as well as the students, ____ excited about the trip.
questions.explanation: 'As well as' does not make the subject plural; 'the teacher' is singular.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I would rather you ____ me the truth now.
questions.explanation: 'Would rather + subject' takes the past form to refer to the present or future.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The suspect denied ____ the money.
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund (-ing form).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Twenty kilometres ____ a long way to walk.
questions.explanation: A distance treated as a single amount takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: It is high time we ____ for the examination.
questions.explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by the past simple with present meaning.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The police ____ arrested the suspects.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun in English: the police have.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Kunle is senior ____ me by two years.
questions.explanation: 'Senior', 'junior', 'superior' and 'inferior' take 'to', not 'than'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She insisted that he ____ the report before Friday.
questions.explanation: After 'insist that', the subjunctive (base form) is used: that he submit.
